screens.title: Virtual Environments with venv and virtualenv
screens.narratorSegment: In professional Python development you will often work on multiple projects that need different versions of the same libraries. Virtual environments let each project live in its own bubble with its own interpreter and site-packages, preventing one project's dependencies from breaking another's. In this lesson we will build a clear habit: create an environment for each project, activate it, install dependencies there, then deactivate when finished. You will practice the built-in venv commands, learn when virtualenv is useful, and see how verifying with pip list proves isolation. A concrete scenario: two projects requiring different Django versions can both run on the same machine if each uses its own virtual environment. Common mistakes are easy to make—forgetting to activate before installing, creating environments inside each other, or committing the environment directory to version control. By the end of these screens you'll know the exact commands to create, activate, install into, and remove virtual environments, and you'll understand why these steps are essential for reproducible development and deployment. Keep an eye out for the activation prompt so you always know which environment you're in.

screens.title: Why virtual environments exist
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual environments exist to solve a practical and common problem: multiple projects on one machine needing different versions of the same library. Imagine Project A requires Django 2.2 while Project B requires Django 3.2. If you install both versions globally, you will overwrite one with the other and risk breaking one project. A virtual environment creates an isolated Python install with its own site-packages directory so each project can have exactly the versions it needs. Technically, activation modifies PATH and shell variables so python and pip reference the environment's interpreter and tools. A clear example: create two folders, make separate environments, install Flask 1.1.2 in one and Flask 2.0.0 in the other, and use pip list to show different outputs. A common misconception is that virtual environments change the system Python — they do not. They simply provide a per-project interpreter and packages while leaving the system install intact. Another misconception is that virtual environments are heavy; in reality venv is lightweight, setting up a minimal structure of bin or Scripts, a lib/site-packages directory, and a small configuration file. Key takeaway: environments protect project stability and make deployments reproducible. Ask yourself: which projects on your machine could break without this isolation?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A virtual environment is a lightweight, isolated Python environment with its own interpreter and site-packages so projects don't conflict.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why virtual environments exist

The conflict problem

Different projects often require different library versions. Installing everything globally causes overwrite conflicts and unstable projects. The virtual environment isolates a project's packages so they do not affect other projects or the system Python.

Example: ProjectA requires Django 2.2; ProjectB requires Django 3.2. Each gets its own environment and both coexist on the same machine.
Common mistake: installing without activating. That installs globally and does not help isolation.
Key Takeaway

Treat a virtual environment as the source of truth for a project’s dependencies so the project behaves consistently on other machines.

Anatomy quick view

A typical venv contains a small directory tree: a bin or Scripts folder with the python and pip executables, a lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages folder for installed packages, and a config file that points to the Python version used.
bin/ or Scripts/ — the environment's executables
lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages — where installed dependencies live
pyvenv.cfg — small config file describing the environment
Misconception check: The environment does not change system packages; it only adjusts PATH while active so commands use the environment's Python.

screens.title: Create a virtual environment with venv
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a virtual environment with venv is a single, repeatable command. From your project's root directory run Python three -m venv. venv to create a directory called. venv containing a minimal Python installation and the layout needed for per-project packages. Using. venv is a convention that keeps the folder hidden in many file browsers, but you may choose another name. After creation you will see a bin or Scripts folder and a lib folder for site-packages. This step does not automatically activate the environment. Creating is separate from activating; many developers script creation as part of project setup and then activate manually when they work. A concrete example: mkdir my_python_project; cd my_python_project; Python three -m venv. venv. Inspecting the tree shows. venv/bin/python,. venv/bin/pip, and. venv/lib/pythonX. Y/site-packages. Misconception to avoid: creating an environment does not install your project dependencies — you must activate and then run pip install or pip install -r requirements. txt. Key takeaway: creation is fast and lightweight, and it's the first reproducible step for consistent development. Create a virtual environment with venv means python3 -m venv .venv creates a local, reproducible environment directory with its own interpreter and package path.. In practical terms, exact commands and directory outcome for a project venv. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Create a venv

Create: exact steps

Use the Python module to create a local environment folder inside the project. Choose a name like .venv to keep it out of sight in many file explorers.
# create and inspect
mkdir my_python_project
cd my_python_project
python3 -m venv .venv
# the .venv folder now contains bin/ or Scripts/, lib/, and pyvenv.cfg
Tip: Use .venv so tools and editors can auto-detect and avoid committing it to git.

Directory outcome

bin/ or Scripts/ — environment executables including python and pip
lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages — where installed packages are placed
pyvenv.cfg — configuration file stating the base interpreter
Misconception

Creating the venv does not install project packages automatically; you must activate it and run pip install or pip install -r requirements.txt.

This visual cue is crucial: it confirms that pip install will target the environment's site-packages and not the global site. Deactivation is simple: run deactivate and the prompt will return to its prior state. A concrete example: after activation run pip install requests and then pip list to confirm requests is listed. Run deactivate and then pip list again to confirm it is absent globally unless previously installed. A common misconception is to think activation copies files into the project — it does not. keyIdea.title: Activation commands
keyIdea.text: source .venv/bin/activate (macOS/Linux); .venv\Scripts\activate.bat (CMD); .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 (PowerShell). Use deactivate to return to global Python.

content.html:
Process Flow › Activate & Deactivate

Activation commands

# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

# Windows (Command Prompt)
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat

# Windows (PowerShell)
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Deactivate the environment
 deactivate
Note the difference between creation and activation: creating adds files; activation changes your shell for the session only.

Visual confirmation

When active you typically see an indicator like (.venv) at the start of your prompt. Always verify before installing packages so you don't pollute your global environment.
Install while active: pip install requests — this places requests inside the venv's site-packages.
Verify: pip list shows installed packages for the active environment.
Misconception check: activation is not permanent. It only applies to the current shell session and must be re-run in new terminals.

screens.title: Install packages and verify isolation
screens.narratorSegment: Installing packages into an active virtual environment is the practical test of isolation. After you activate the environment, pip will default to the environment's pip and install packages into lib/site-packages there. A concrete walkthrough: activate your. venv, run pip install requests, and then run pip list to observe requests in the list. Now deactivate and run pip list again in the global shell; requests should not appear unless it was installed globally before. This process proves that the package lives only inside the environment. A common mistake is to run pip install in the wrong shell or to have multiple python executables and mistakenly use a global pip. If you suspect that, run which python or where python to confirm the path points inside the venv. Another useful command for reproducibility is pip freeze > requirements. txt after installing the packages; that file records exact versions for deployment and for teammates to recreate the environment. Key takeaway: always verify installation with pip list and export requirements to ensure reproducibility. Install packages and verify isolation means activate, pip install the package, run pip list to confirm it appears, then deactivate and check global pip list to confirm isolation.. In practical terms, pip install inside an active venv and checking with pip list. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Activate, pip install the package, run pip list to confirm it appears, then deactivate and check global pip list to confirm isolation.

content.html:
Definition › Install & Verify

Walkthrough commands

# activate, install, verify
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install requests
pip list
# expected in the environment's pip list: requests

deactivate
pip list
# expected in global pip list: requests NOT listed (unless previously installed globally)
If requests appears in global pip list after deactivation, it means it was previously installed globally — the environment still provided isolation for the new install during activation.

Reproducibility

Export your environment with pip freeze > requirements.txt. That requirements file lets others create the same environment with pip install -r requirements.txt on a fresh venv.
Tip: After adding packages, run pip freeze > requirements.txt to capture exact versions.
Check path: run which python or where python to ensure commands target the venv's interpreter.
Misconception check: pip install does not automatically know which project you meant unless the environment is active in the shell where you run it.

screens.title: venv vs virtualenv
screens.narratorSegment: venv is the built-in module in Python three.3 and later and is sufficient for most modern projects. It is lightweight, easy to use, and requires no additional installation. virtualenv is a third-party tool that predates venv; it remains useful when you need broader compatibility, such as working with Python 2 or older Python three versions, or when you need advanced options to choose a non-default interpreter. To install virtualenv you use pip install virtualenv globally and then create an environment with virtualenv my_project_env. Activation and deactivation behave the same as venv. A concrete contrast: if you have multiple Python interpreters installed and need to point the environment to a specific interpreter binary, virtualenv historically provided finer control. A common misconception is that virtualenv is always better — it is not. For new Python three projects, venv is preferred because it is built-in and simpler. Another misconception is that venv cannot be used in production; it can be used wherever you can run Python. Key takeaway: choose venv for most cases; keep virtualenv in your toolbox for legacy compatibility or special interpreter control.

content.html:
Comparison › venv vs virtualenv

venv (built-in)

Included with Python 3.3+. Lightweight and recommended for new projects using modern Python. No extra install step is required.
Create: python3 -m venv .venv
Activation: source .venv/bin/activate or Windows variants

virtualenv (third-party)

Install with pip install virtualenv and create with virtualenv my_project_env. Useful for older Python versions or when you must select a specific interpreter binary explicitly.
Install: pip install virtualenv
Create: virtualenv my_project_env
When to prefer virtualenv

Prefer virtualenv when working with legacy interpreters or when you need advanced environment creation options. Otherwise use venv for simplicity and built-in support.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes cause confusion but are easy to avoid with a few habits. First, forgetting to activate before installing will put packages into the global environment, risking conflicts. Always check the prompt for the environment name and run which python if unsure. Second, creating a virtual environment inside another environment can cause unexpected behavior and nested PATH references; create environments at the project root instead. Third, do not commit the environment directory to version control — it is large and reproducible from requirements. txt. Add. venv/ or your chosen env folder to. gitignore. Fourth, rely on requirements. txt for reproducibility: after installing packages, run pip freeze > requirements. txt and commit that file. For deployment, create a fresh environment on the server and run pip install -r requirements. txt to match versions exactly. Finally, watch for platform-specific activation differences on Windows and POSIX systems. Key takeaway: adopt simple rules — activate before install, keep venv out of source control, export requirements, and create environments at the project root. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process › Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common pitfalls

  • Forgetting to activate before pip install installs packages globally.
  • Creating an environment inside another environment causes nested PATH confusion.
  • Committing the environment directory to Git rather than using requirements.txt.

Practical habits

  • Add .venv/ to .gitignore and commit requirements.txt instead.
  • Run which python to confirm the active interpreter during setup.
  • Create environments at project root and re-activate each new terminal session.
Key Takeaway

Simple, repeatable habits prevent most virtual environment issues: activate, verify, export, and ignore the env directory in source control.

You will practice the built-in venv commands, learn when virtualenv is useful, and see how verifying with pip list proves isolation. Common mistakes are easy to make—forgetting to activate before installing, creating environments inside each other, or committing the environment directory to version control. Knowing when to prefer virtualenv is a judgment based on compatibility needs; you'll practice the exact installation and creation commands for virtualenv so you can handle legacy projects. These objectives matter because dependency conflicts are common in multi-project workflows and in deployment. Let's summarize three essential concepts to keep top of mind. First, a virtual environment is an isolated Python environment with its own interpreter and site-packages so you can manage per-project dependencies without conflict. Second, venv is the built-in, modern, and usually preferred tool for creating environments; it is lightweight and works well for Python three projects. Third, activation temporarily changes your shell so python and pip reference the environment; always verify with the prompt indicator and which python to ensure you're operating in the intended environment. These three items — isolation, tool choice, and activation verification — are foundational habits that will make your development and deployments far more reliable. Practice them until activation and pip verification are second nature. Three more practical reminders will keep your workflows smooth. First, never commit your environment directory; instead, add it to. gitignore and commit requirements. txt created with pip freeze. Second, know when to use virtualenv — mainly for legacy Python versions or special interpreter control — but prefer venv for new Python three projects. Third, reproduce environments on servers by creating a venv on the server and running pip install -r requirements. txt so production matches development. These rules reduce accidental global installs, simplify onboarding for teammates, and make deployments reliable.
